title: US voters roundly reject data centers in ballot measures
titleZh: US voters roundly reject data centers in ballot measures
author: justonepost2
relevanceReason: 命中 1 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryRaw: American voters roundly rejected data centers nearly anywhere they were on the ballot Tuesday, a rebuke sure to rattle investors already growing skittish about the AI buildout. Residents in more than 30 localities across nine states voted for moratoriums, outright bans, and other measures, some in direct response to specific projects underway. Edgewater, Fla. overwhelmingly voted to embed a data-center ban in the city’s charter, and voters in Perry, Ohio passed a measure placing financial and operational constraints on hyperscalers seeking tax breaks. Democrats running in more than 130 federal and gubernatorial races aired anti-tech or anti-data center ads this cycle, one analysis showed. The pressure pushed some Republican candidates including Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, an AI booster just a few months ago, into promises of tougher regulation; he lost anyway.Banks and asset managers financing the buildout have already begun treating local opposition as a credit risk, while hyperscalers are rushing to hire community liaisons. Meanwhile, tech companies bracing for the vibe shift are trying to rebrand the data centers as “compute campuses” with mixed results, Semafor’s Ashley Gold reported.

comments.author: ndiddy
comments.textRawHtml:
A lot of people here are portraying the opposition to data centers as being uneducated hypocrites who are against anything getting built. When you look at what the opposition are saying, they generally know what they are talking about. Here's Abdul El-Sayed (new Michigan senator) talking about his ideas for regulating the AI industry: https://youtu.be/YX44XDt0gXI?t=182 . For datacenters specifically, he isn't against them being built but thinks that there need to be rules in place so the communities that they're being built in actually benefit from them. He views moratoriums as something that localities and states should be doing until those rules are in place federally. The rules he suggests are:

- There must be community benefits agreements negotiated transparently with the local community

- Any new datacenters being built cannot raise utility rates

- Some of the revenue generated by the datacenter must be set aside to improve power reliability

- Datacenters must not touch our waterways at all

- Datacenters must be built using union labor

A lot of the communities that had datacenters built in them ended up getting steamrolled in negotiations by the tech companies because you had the local government (in small towns, this is people who work part time making a few thousand dollars per year) negotiating a deal with the Google/xAI/Oracle/etc corporate lawyers. I think it makes sense to say that the buildout should be paused until fairer terms can be worked out on a national level, rather than letting this continue to happen.

children.author: pj_mukh
children.textRawHtml:
>>“- There must be community benefits agreements negotiated transparently with the local community

- Any new datacenters being built cannot raise utility rates

- Some of the revenue generated by the datacenter must be set aside to improve power reliability

- Datacenters must not touch our waterways at all

- Datacenters must be built using union labor”

Deal. This sounds like a great list. I would add, “no property tax breaks”.

Just get the state to pass this as a law and set appropriate enforcement mechanisms and then just let data centers go ham if they meet this criteria?

No more “per community meetings” and municipal haggling (see: corrupting) local governments. Buy the land build the data centers. The municipality can figure out the exact benefits that works for that community from the giant tax coffers.

This seems imminently fair to me.

children.author: ethbr1
children.textRawHtml:
Regulated monopolies can be more efficient than state ownership... if the regulatory framework has the correct incentives. Unfortunately, that's very hard to do.

The benefit with regulated monopolies are that you have a separation of control between regulation (from PSC/voters) and monopoly (running its business).

If the current regulatory regime isn't producing the desired results, it can be changed.

With straight state ownership, things are much more entangled.

children.author: throwaway5752
children.textRawHtml:
I don't think people are a ignorant or provincial as people here are suggesting.

Broadly, the people in areas with datacenters understand that AI is leading to a loss of control and concentration in power and money. A lot of people in these rural areas have been on the receiving end of this sort of screw job for generations. Their skepticism is earned, and the way our field has tried to ram these projects through with what I will try to gently call a "ship it" ethos has not helped.

This is probably a healthy reset for the field overall, and for the country. A number of the leadership of these companies have seemed to develop manifest destiny or messiah complexes that are offputting to most people. Polling data supports this.

It's a local problem., but it's not just a local problem.

children.author: rainsford
children.textRawHtml:
I would love it if this type of thing convinced the AI people they need to take a different approach to their business and marketing. Right now their sales pitch is basically we know it might suck having a data center in your backyard and it's a major bummer that any product involving a computer chip is vastly more expensive for the first time ever, but on the other hand our new AI technology is going to take your job and maybe destroy humanity.

I'm sure these guys aren't dumb, but they certainly act pretty dumb. What really solidified it for me was the choice they made to build data centers literally right next to neighborhoods and then run incredibly loud gas turbine generators 24/7. Even if they were legally allowed to do that, how they did they imagine it would go explicitly signalling that they couldn't give two shits about people living in the community? It's definitely some combination of incompetence and hubris to not predict the resulting backlash.

That's nice list, but it doesn't go far enough. It only addresses problems with the data centers themselves, but they are also a point of leverage against the entire AI industry. It's that industry that makes them so controversial and hated. If they were just power-hungry factories making bolts or solar panels or something, no one would care.
